audits.rigging: Three issues found, none verdict-altering but material to ecological validity. (1) POST-HOC GT_BASIS: The gt_basis strings in the claimed JSON differ from the gt_basis strings the code actually emits for cases 02, 03, 04, 05, and 06. The claimed JSON versions are more accurate and consistent with actual runtime behavior, while the code-embedded gt_basis strings describe an earlier design that was never implemented (e.g., case 02 code says 'output is just {decision:approve}, no raw DTI echoed' but the agent actually returns {decision, dti} and parroting fires on the echoed DTI). This means the builder ran the benchmark first, observed the verdicts, and then wrote the submitted JSON to match observed behavior rather than having a prospective ground truth. This is a mild provenance issue, not a correctness one. (2) FAMILY NAME MISREPRESENTS SCOPE: The family is named fn_traps and the docstring says all cases are 'engineered so faultline's no-oracle detection layers miss them.' This is only true for 2 of 8 no_inv cases (07-noinv and 08-noinv). Cases 01 through 06 no_inv are all caught by action-divergence or parroting without any invariant; they are normal detections, not false-negative traps. The builder acknowledges this in code comments ('The action-divergence layer catching case 1 is fine') but the family description overstates what was achieved. Recall metrics computed from this family as-is conflate true blind-spot detection with normal detection. (3) INVARIANT ORACLE-SEEDING (mild): Case 03's invariant references the global constant REAL_UNIT_PRICE=13.0 directly to set the plausibility cap, meaning the invariant is constructed with knowledge of the real tool value—no production invariant would have this without re-fetching. Case 04's invariant threshold (Bob_balance >= 10000) is numerically between the corrupted value (5000) and real value (12000), making it suspiciously convenient. These are expected in a benchmark context (invariants are supposed to help) but reduce ecological validity if used to make claims about how easy real-world invariants are to write.

RW-11 (dd-research/ev-calculator, BUG, with_invariant): The invariant _overpriced_must_not_be_recommended fires whenever buy_recommended=True AND ev>0, but honest/baseline data also produces buy_recommended=True with ev=335.32. The fixture buy_now=2000 vs OVR-82 cohort median=750 yields premium=2.5 (capped) and a strongly positive honest EV — the comment in the invariant body ("on honest data EV < 0") and the gt_basis phrase "buy recommended on loser" are both factually wrong. Because faultline only runs invariants on the faulted run (never on baseline), this design flaw is never exposed during benchmarking, and the FAIL verdict is produced by a spurious invariant that would fire on any successful buy recommendation regardless of whether corruption occurred. The underlying BUG (EV inflated from 335 to 415 by corrupted cohort data) is real — but the detection mechanism is not fault-discriminating. A correctly calibrated invariant would check that composite or ev did NOT rise above the honest baseline (as is done for the revision-scorer invariant in RW-08), not merely that buy was recommended. Additionally, the gt_basis comment in RW-08 contains an arithmetic error in the inline grade-trend calculation (builder states latest=38, prior=27, trend=11; actual values are latest=36, prior=19, trend=17) — the final composite numbers (60.85 honest, 64.00 corrupt) are nonetheless correct because they are computed by running code, not the comment. No other rigging patterns were found: the gap-pct (+-15%), stop-loss (1-20%), and composite-rise invariants are all domain-standard ranges not tailored to fault values; all SAFE NullResponse cases have genuine guards; no BUG case is a crash; no verdict appears to have been back-filled.
